analysis.one_liner: Requires every bank to offer a low-fee basic checking account to people with low and moderate incomes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after two days of Senate subcommittee hearings in June 1989, it sat in the Banking Committee until the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every federally insured bank, savings institution, and credit union to offer a 'basic financial services account' to people with $1,000 or less on deposit. The account could require no more than a $25 minimum opening deposit, could charge a maintenance fee no higher than the bank's actual processing costs as set by the Federal Reserve, and had to allow at least 10 withdrawals a month, including checks, with no requirement to use only ATMs [S3]. Banks would have had to post notices about the account, and regulators could enforce the rules, with customers able to sue for violations [S3]. It never reached the full Senate [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income people who are unbanked or pay high fees: they would gain access to a no-frills checking account with at most a $25 minimum, at least 10 withdrawals a month, teller access (not ATM-only), and fees capped at the bank's actual processing costs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Every federally insured depository institution must offer a basic account available to individuals with $1,000 or less on deposit, with no minimum opening or ongoing balance above $25 [S3].
Maintenance fees, including all service charges for routine transactions, may not exceed a minimal, reasonable amount the Federal Reserve sets based on the bank's actual net processing costs [S3].

Accounts must permit at least 10 withdrawals per month, including checks or similar instruments where the institution offers them, and cannot force customers to use only ATMs or require other account relationships [S3].

Banks must post conspicuous notices describing the account's features and provide written summaries on request, and customers can bring civil actions with statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 plus attorney's fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other depository institutions, which would have to serve low-balance customers at fees capped near their actual processing costs, could face enforcement actions and civil suits, and would bear compliance costs for notices, registration, and summaries [S3].

drawbacks.text: Banks would be required to serve a customer base with balances of $1,000 or less at fees capped near their own processing costs, a mandate they could argue forces them to subsidize accounts and could lead them to raise fees on other customers [S3].

The bill relies on the Federal Reserve and banking regulators to define 'minimal, reasonable' fees and to enforce compliance, so its protections would depend heavily on how regulators write and apply the rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: millions of households without bank accounts rely on costly check-cashing and money-order services, and a low-fee account with teller access would cut those costs. The cost falls on banks, which would have to offer these accounts at roughly their own processing cost, and possibly indirectly on other customers through fee adjustments. The bill's main weakness is that its key term — a fee limited to 'actual' processing costs — would be defined by regulators, leaving room for weak implementation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and got two days of hearings in a consumer subcommittee in June 1989, but the full committee never acted and it died there when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on May 3, 1989; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
The committee had no cosponsors: the cosponsor page shows zero [S4].
On June 6-7, 1989, the Banking Committee's Subcommittee on Consumer and Regulatory Affairs held hearings on the bill, which were printed as S.Hrg. 101-471 — the only action it ever received [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the bill remained in committee until the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other depository institutions are better off: they never had to offer no-frills accounts at fees capped at their own processing costs, and unbanked low-income households kept bearing the cost of check-cashing and money-order alternatives.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks that avoided the low-fee mandate

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; it had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force every federally insured bank, savings institution, and credit union to offer a no-frills account with a maximum $25 minimum and fees capped at the institution's own processing costs — near-zero-margin business — plus civil liability for violations [S3]. The industry would gain some depositors it does not currently serve, but its interest in blocking the bill ran against low-income people's interest in affordable accounts.

industries.industry: Check cashers and fee-based money service providers
industries.note: Households without bank accounts pay check-cashing and money-order fees for basic transactions; a low-fee bank account with at least 10 withdrawals and check-writing per month would directly reduce that market [S3].
